name: Nanai of the Kur river / Kur-Urmi dialect
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Sunik, O. P. 1948. O jazyke nanajcev na r. Kure [О языке нанайцев на р. Куре]. Izvestija Akademii nauk SSSR, Otdelenie literatury i jazyka 7(6): 537-550.
catalog_locator: p. 541, phonetics section, penultimate paragraph; summary item 4 on p. 542; restated p. 550
catalog_quote: Что касается ударения в слове, то оно на слух ничем не отличается от того, что наблюдается в других нанайских говорах. Вопрос о лексическом ударении в нанайском языке пока по-настоящему (экспериментально-фонетически) не исследован. Можно думать, что слабое экспираторное ударение падает в нанайском на первый слог; последний же слог слова имеет тоническое (музыкальное) ударение — незначительное повышение тона. Для слуха русских именно это последнее тоническое ударение оказывается наиболее заметным. Обычно оно и отмечается без указания на особый его характер, т. е. отмечается как привычное для русской речи экспираторное ударение, но в отличие от русского не свободное, а связанное: всегда на последнем слоге слова. [p. 542] 4. Словесное ударение общенанайского типа.

new_statements.translation: As for stress in the word, to the ear it does not differ in any way from what is observed in the other Nanai dialects. The question of lexical stress in Nanai has not yet been properly (experimentally-phonetically) investigated. One may think that a weak expiratory stress falls in Nanai on the first syllable, while the last syllable of the word has a tonic (musical) accent — a slight rise of pitch. [...] Usually it is this [final tonic accent] that is marked, without indication of its special character, i.e. it is marked as the expiratory stress familiar from Russian speech, but unlike Russian it is not free but bound: always on the last syllable of the word.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Kur Nanai is of the 'general Nanai type' (Sunik's summary item 4, p. 542): the perceptible, conventionally marked prominence is a bound pitch rise on the final syllable of the word regardless of morphology; Sunik additionally hypothesises a weak dynamic (expiratory) stress on the first syllable. Reading chosen = fixed: final syllable (the bound final accent, matching Avrorin 1959: 62-63 for Nanai); an alternative coding is fixed: initial syllable dynamic + final tonal accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the weak initial expiratory stress Sunik posits alongside the final tonic accent is the only second prominence mentioned.
new_statements.exceptions: None; explicitly 'не свободное, а связанное: всегда на последнем слоге слова'. Sunik stresses that lexical stress in Nanai had not been studied instrumentally (as of 1948).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (ударение в слове / словесное ударение), impressionistic ('на слух'), from Sunik's own fieldwork on the Nanai of the Kur river (villages near Ulika); no instrumental data; the 1958 monograph may refine it.
new_statements.identity_note: Sunik 1948 describes the speech of the Nanai of the Kur river (Kur-Urmi dialect / Kili), i.e. Glottolog kuro1242 proper. Glottolog separates the Chinese Hezhen 'Qileng' variety as Kilen [kile1243]; the only modern grammar for that variety (Zhang 2013, held by the project under kile1243) reports initial root stress, which differs from Sunik's final-accent description, so the two glottocodes should not be merged for stress.

sources.citation: Zhang, Paiyu. 2013. The Kilen language of Manchuria: grammar of a moribund Tungusic language. PhD thesis, University of Hong Kong. §2.3.5 Stress, p. 41.
sources.note: 'Generally, the lexical roots of Kilen are stressed on the first syllable'; secondary stress in words of four or more syllables (compounds: first syllable of the last polysyllabic component; inflected forms: first syllable of a polysyllabic suffix chain). Describes the Chinese Hezhen 'Qileng' variety = Glottolog kile1243, not the Russian Kur-Urmi.

sources.citation: Avrorin, V. A. 1959. Grammatika nanajskogo jazyka, t. 1. Moskva-Leningrad: AN SSSR, pp. 62-63 ('Ударение').
sources.note: General (literary/Naikhin) Nanai: stress is mixed musical-dynamic, mainly a pitch rise with slight intensity, and 'строго регулярным, связанным — оно всегда падает на последний слог слова'. This is the 'general-Nanai type' Sunik 1948 says Kur-Urmi shares.
